title: Phonetics · L1 Introduction to the IPA

questions.stem: Why does English need a phonetic alphabet, according to the lecture?
options: The same letters can correspond to different sounds
The same sound can be written in different ways
Medical terms come from Greek and Latin roots whose spelling doesn't match ordinary English patterns
English spelling represents pronunciation perfectly
questions.explanation: English spelling only partially represents pronunciation; a phonetic alphabet assigns exactly one symbol to each distinct sound.

questions.stem: Match the branch of phonetics to what it studies:
options: Auditory — how sounds are perceived by the listener
Acoustic — how sounds are transmitted as sound waves
Articulatory — how sounds are produced by the vocal organs
Auditory — how sounds are produced by the larynx
questions.explanation: Phonetics studies physical properties of speech sounds in three branches; this course focuses on articulatory phonetics.

questions.stem: Why does the course focus on articulatory phonetics?
options: It studies sound waves with instruments
It is the only branch of phonetics
It is the branch most directly useful for improving a learner's own pronunciation
It replaces phonology
questions.explanation: Articulatory phonetics deals with sound production by the vocal organs, which is what learners need to change their pronunciation.

options: It studies sound waves
It studies how sounds function within a particular language's sound system
It asks which sound differences change meaning
Its basic unit is the phoneme
questions.explanation: Phonology studies which sound differences change meaning; its basic unit is the phoneme. Sound waves belong to acoustic phonetics.

options: A sound variant that never changes meaning
Shown inside square brackets in narrow transcription
The same thing as a letter of the alphabet
The smallest unit of sound that can distinguish one word from another
questions.explanation: /p/ and /b/ are separate phonemes because pin and bin are different words. A variant that never changes meaning is an allophone.

questions.stem: The p in "pin" and the p in "spin":
options: Are two different phonemes because they sound slightly different
Are allophones of the same phoneme /p/
Differ because the first is aspirated and the second is not
Are perceived by English speakers as the same sound
questions.explanation: Allophones are different phonetic realizations of one phoneme that never change meaning on their own.

questions.stem: About slant brackets and square brackets:
options: [pʰɪn] is a narrow (phonetic) transcription
/pɪn/ is a broad (phonemic) transcription
The ʰ in [pʰɪn] marks aspiration
This course mostly uses square brackets
questions.explanation: The course uses broad (slant-bracket) transcription for most purposes, keeping square brackets for specific phonetic detail.

options: /pen/
[pʰen]
/tiːm/
[tʰiːm]
questions.explanation: Square brackets + the aspiration diacritic = narrow. Slant brackets = broad.

options: It was developed by the International Phonetic Association
Each symbol always represents the same sound
It is language-independent
Vowel symbols are easy to predict from ordinary spelling
questions.explanation: Vowel symbols are less predictable from spelling and must be learned individually.

questions.stem: Which IPA consonant symbols does the lecture describe as unfamiliar (not ordinary Latin letters)?
options: ʃ
ŋ
k
θ
questions.explanation: /p, b, t, d, k, g, m, n, l, r/ look like Latin letters; /θ, ð, ʃ, ʒ, ŋ/ are borrowed from Greek or specially designed.

questions.stem: Match the word to its spelling difficulty as given in the lecture:
options: psychology — silent initial "p"
stomach — "ch" represents /k/
pharmacy — "ph" represents /f/
muscle — silent "m"
questions.explanation: In muscle /ˈmʌsl/ it's the "c" that is silent.

options: cog
cuff
cough
calf

questions.stem: Match the transcription to the word:
options: /ɡɔːz/ — gauze
/jɔːn/ — yawn
/θʌm/ — thumb
/haɪt/ — heat
questions.explanation: /haɪt/ is height (the diphthong aɪ as in "high").

questions.stem: The four words though, cough, through and enough show that:
options: English spelling is a reliable guide to pronunciation
The IPA gives each sound one symbol regardless of spelling
One spelling pattern ("-ough") can have four different pronunciations
"-ough" is always pronounced /ɒf/
